articles.author: Rachel Carlson
articles.description: The release of Dr. Anthony Fauci's pandemic diaries has rekindled the debate over the origins of SARS-CoV-2. Here's how scientists have weighed in.
articles.title: Animal spillover? Lab leak? What the science says about the origins of COVID-19

articles.author: Sydney Lupkin
articles.description: Federal subsidies that have helped defray insurers' Medicare drug costs will disappear at the end of the year. Millions of beneficiaries could face higher premiums in 2027.
articles.title: The Trump administration's move to end subsidies for Medicare drug plans could cost consumers

articles.author: Kirk Siegler
articles.description: Wildfires in central and eastern Oregon are prompting evacuations and forcing ranchers to scramble to move cattle and find feed as public range land burns. More than a million acres have burned so far. Most fires have little or no containment.
articles.title: Oregon is on track for its worst wildfire season yet

articles.author: Jan Camenzind Broomby
articles.description: The author and translator of Taiwan Travelogue, the winner of the 2026 International Booker Prize, discuss identity and history amid the debate over Taiwan's colonial ties to Japan and escalating geopolitical pressure from China.
articles.title: 'Taiwan Travelogue' rethinks history, colonialism, and identity

articles.author: Dave Davies
articles.description: The renowned classics scholar caused a stir when her critical review of Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey went viral. Wilson explains her reaction to the film and why she's translating the poem again.
articles.title: 'Odyssey' translator Emily Wilson says Nolan shouldn't have written the movie himself

articles.author: Betsy Joles
articles.description: Chitral borders Afghanistan and isn't easy to reach. Breathtaking views abound in this remote mountainous region — as do rockslides and avalanches.
articles.title: Greetings from an isolated region in northern Pakistan's Hindu Kush mountains

articles.author: Stephen Thompson
articles.description: Glen Hansard, the Irish singer who won an Oscar for the musical movie Once and the led the bands The Frames and The Swell Season, died on Wednesday. He died following a motorcycle crash in Dublin.
articles.title: Glen Hansard, Irish songwriter and 'Once' star, dies at 56

articles.author: The Associated Press
articles.description: A school district in upstate New York is pausing plans to deploy an AI-powered, humanoid robot in the classroom after state education officials, teachers and local residents raised concerns.
articles.title: New York school pauses plan to deploy humanlike AI robot teacher after backlash

articles.author: The Associated Press
articles.description: The flare-up on multiple fronts raised the risk of a return to all-out war, underscoring the difficulty of winding down a five-month conflict that has jolted the world economy.
articles.title: Iran resumes missile attacks as U.S. and Saudis strike Tehran-backed militias in Iraq

articles.author: Chloe Veltman
articles.description: "What is beyond reality?" asks artist Refik Anadol. His latest projects include Dataland, an immersive AI art museum in Los Angeles, and an installation at the Smithsonian in Washington, D.C.
articles.title: 'Machines are collaborators' at this new museum of AI art

articles.author: Guardian staff and agencies
articles.description:
Soldiers and emergency workers are combing through a badly damaged shopping mall and collapsed houses looking for trapped survivors
The death toll from the major earthquake that hit Japan on Tuesday rose to at least 23 as the search for trapped survivors inside a badly damaged shopping mall and collapsed houses in the country’s south-west continued.
The magnitude 6.8 earthquake that struck the Kumamoto prefecture on the island of Kyushu has injured at least 62, the prefectural government said. That number has steadily grown, fanning fears it will rise.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Death toll in Japan earthquake rises to 17 as aftershock and heat complicate rescue efforts

articles.author: Nick Visser
articles.description:
Follow updates live

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Minister says meeting Closing the Gap target a major step, but more work needed on others
Malarndirri McCarthy, the minister for Indigenous Australians, said early childhood education enrolment for First Nations children was a milestone in the effort to reach the Closing the Gap targets.
It is important to see this milestone achieved, and that is because of the work of the Aboriginal and community controlled sector and those involved in the preschool sector. … Clearly, the challenges with all the other targets remain, but I do take heart at the fact that this has been achieved.
It’s very, very difficult to deal with these situations where you have particular pieces of legislation that see the high incarceration rates of First Nations people. What that means is that we have to go harder, we have to keep pushing the states and territories around the justice factors. Clearly, that is a real concern.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Australia news live: Icac witness compares Liberal factional fighting to Braveheart; Acma takes Optus to court over triple-zero outage

articles.author: Adam Fulton
articles.description:
US says attacks on Thursday morning hit dozens of Revolutionary Guard targets while experts say earlier strikes by both sides increase risk of return to all-out war

US-Saudi strikes in Iraq push region into ‘uncharted territory’, analysts warn

The US military is saying is has finished its “heavy wave of strikes” against Iran.
Central Command said in a statement posted on X that it struck “dozens of Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets in Iran, including military command centers, missile and drone facilities, coastal surveillance and defense sites, and maritime capabilities”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Middle East crisis live: US launches ‘heavy waves of strikes’ on Iran after days-long pause in attacks

articles.author: Guardian staff and agencies
articles.description:
Fires across the Ukrainian capital after ballistic missile attack, while Kyiv’s forces continue cross-border attacks with another Wildberries warehouse hit
Russian strikes on Kyiv killed at least one person, authorities said on Thursday, after the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, issued a warning ahead of Moscow launching another massive attack.
“Sadly, one death has been confirmed,” the Kyiv city military administration announced. Kyiv mayor, Vitali Klitschko, reported fires in several districts of the city. Earlier, he posted: “The enemy is attacking the capital with ballistic weapons. The threat of further attack remains present. Stay in shelters!”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Deadly strikes on Kyiv after Zelenskyy warns of ‘massive’ Russian attack

articles.author: Josh Butler
articles.description:
LNP member Llew O’Brien says ‘there is nothing wrong with being proud of your heritage’, leading Angus Taylor to state: ‘I congratulate all Australians’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Federal Coalition MP Llew O’Brien has declared it’s “encouraging to see a White Australian” win a sprinting medal at the Commonwealth Games, after Lachlan Kennedy took silver when setting a new national record in Glasgow.
O’Brien, the member for Wide Bay in Queensland, wrote on social media on Wednesday: “White Men Can Sprint!”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Queensland MP pens ‘White Men Can Sprint’ social media post after Lachlan Kennedy takes silver in Glasgow

articles.author: Benita Kolovos Victorian state correspondent
articles.description:
New Victorian premier also considering ‘sensible changes’ to laws that would enshrine right to work from home two days a week

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Victoria’s new premier has not ruled out redirecting billions of dollars earmarked for the controversial Suburban Rail Loop to other projects, saying he’s seeking to pursue the “greatest value for Victorians”.
Ben Carroll also used his second day in the top job to flag “sensible changes” to nation-leading laws that would enshrine the right to work from home two days a week, as he tries to distance himself from predecessors Jacinta Allan and Daniel Andrews.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ben Carroll will not rule out redirecting Suburban Rail Loop funds to other projects

articles.author: Robert Mackey, Lucy Campbell, Jo Walters, Rachel Leingang and Tom Ambrose
articles.description:
This blog is now closed. You can read our latest story here

Sign up for US Breaking News email

Gary Peters, the Democratic ranking member on the homeland security committee, said that the committee has a long history of bipartisan inquiry and oversight, and the subject matter of risky research and the origins of covid-19 are a legitimate area to study.
But today’s hearing with Anthony Fauci was not an example of that, Peters said.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Senate committee delays vote on Todd Blanche attorney general nomination – as it happened

articles.author: Donna Lu
articles.description:
Authorities say local transmission of H5 bird flu virus among South Australian birds signals ‘shift in the situation’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australia has entered a new phase in dealing with the incursion of deadly H5N1 bird flu, with authorities confirming on Wednesday that local transmission had taken place, and Victoria confirming first case of the highly virulent strain Thursday.
“We have had what is suggestive of local transmission for the first time,” Julie Collins, the federal minister for agriculture, fisheries and forestry, said on Wednesday afternoon, after 11 suspected detections were reported in South Australian birds.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Bird flu has reached Victoria and more wildlife deaths loom. How bad could it get?

articles.author: Josh Butler
articles.description:
Member for Solomon has previously denied alleged incident with administrator David Connolly

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Luke Gosling, the federal Labor member for Solomon, has been arrested over an alleged assault on the Northern Territory’s administrator earlier this month, NT police have said.
“The Northern Territory police force has arrested the 54-year-old federal member for Solomon in relation to an alleged assault on the administrator of the Northern Territory,” police said in a statement.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Federal Labor MP Luke Gosling arrested over alleged assault of NT administrator

articles.author: Sam Levine
articles.description:
Republican John Cornyn says he will not back nomination without written confirmation $1.8bn slush fund is dead
Todd Blanche’s hopes of becoming US attorney general seemed to be in jeopardy on Wednesday after the Department of Justice did not provide written assurances to a key Republican senator that a $1.8bn slush fund was dead.
The US Senate judiciary committee postponed a vote scheduled for Thursday on whether to advance Blanche’s nomination.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump’s pick for US attorney general Todd Blanche in jeopardy as vote postponed

articles.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo and agency
articles.description:
Police link shooting to gang violence but have not said who might have fired bullets that killed bystanders on Sunday
Bullets that fatally struck two bystanders during a shootout at a Seattle food festival last weekend do not appear to have come from the gun that a 15-year-old arrested at the scene was firing, police said in court documents filed on Wednesday.
The teen sprayed an untraceable “ghost gun” into a crowd, authorities say. Preliminary ballistics testing did not match the bullets recovered from the deceased bystanders to that weapon.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Bullets that killed two at Seattle food festival do not match teen shooter’s gun, police say

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
First-in-nation law sets up test on states’ power to regulate use of AI as it tries to outlaw fake nude images of real people
Elon Musk’s company xAI has sued Minnesota over the state’s first-in-the-nation law banning “nudification” technology on websites and apps, potentially providing a test for how far states can go in constitutionally regulating the use of artificial intelligence.
Musk’s company sued on Monday in federal court, days before the law is set to take effect on Saturday and make Minnesota the first state to try to outlaw the increasingly proliferating technology that lets people use AI to create fake nude images of real people. The law was signed in May.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Elon Musk’s xAI sues Minnesota over law banning ‘nudification’ technology

articles.author: Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor
articles.description:
Prime minister to highlight investment in communities as he launches next phase of nuclear submarine replacement
Andy Burnham will place the renewal of Trident at the heart of his vision of a reindustrialised Britain on Thursday when he travels to Barrow-in-Furness to launch the next phase of the nuclear submarine replacement programme.
The new prime minister intends to emphasise that defence spending on projects such as the £31bn Dreadnought-class boats built in the Cumbrian town is a case study of taxpayer investment revitalising communities around the UK.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trident renewal central to defence spending, says Andy Burnham

articles.author: Johana Bhuiyan
articles.description:
Stock tumbles nearly 8% after weaker-than-expected results, despite CEO’s blitz to tout positive effects of AI
Mark Zuckerberg’s media spree touting the positive effects of artificial intelligence did little to cushion the blow of Meta’s second-quarter earnings, which sent its stock tumbling on Wednesday.
In a Wall Street Journal op-ed published on Tuesday, the Meta chief executive expressed his optimism for a world where everyone has access to a super-intelligent machine.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Meta misses earnings forecasts after Zuckerberg media push to promote AI

articles.author: Helena Smith in Athens
articles.description:
Greek authorities identify remains as those of Elizabeth Jane Ross after discovery in a derelict building 11 days ago 
A body found in a suitcase in an abandoned building in central Athens has been identified as that of a 38-year-old British woman.
Eleven days after the find, and following an appeal to foreign law enforcement agencies, Greek police shed some light on the mystery of the body that until Wednesday had remained unidentified.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Body found in suitcase in Athens is that of 38-year-old British woman

articles.author: Aletha Adu Political correspondent
articles.description:
Scotland Yard says threshold not met for criminal action against Green leader, who has refused to apologise to his Reform rival
No further action will be taken by police after Zack Polanski shared a photo of a man with a T-shirt showing a guillotine and the phrase “we’re only making plans for Nigel”.
The Metropolitan police’s decision comes after the Green party leader for England and Wales said he had made an “inadvertent mistake” and would not apologise to Nigel Farage.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Police take no further action over Polanski sharing Farage guillotine image

articles.author: Dan Milmo and Vikram Dodd
articles.description:
Details of parents and staff, including email addresses and phone numbers, are among data taken by cybercriminals
The Department for Education and a police database have been targeted by a cyber-attack, exposing more than 740,000 pieces of data.
Details of government officials, senior school leaders, university staff, police officers and members of the public have been taken by hackers.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Hackers steal sensitive data from UK Department for Education and police

articles.author: Ajit Niranjan and Jennifer Rankin
articles.description:
Repeated heatwaves and strong winds alarm experts, who warn blazes are becoming harder to quell
Three Greek firefighters have died while tackling wildfires on the island of Crete and in the south of the mainland, the Greek fire department has said, as extreme heat hinders efforts to control blazes ravaging southern Europe.
The arc of brutal fires, which runs from the Atlantic coast to the eastern Mediterranean, and from the Scottish Highlands to the south of Spain, has alarmed experts because many of the fires have been out of control and burning close to towns and cities.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Three firefighters killed on Crete and in mainland Greece as Europe battles wildfires

articles.author: Patrick Butler Social policy editor
articles.description:
Rightwing media hostility helped sink his reform plans in 2010, but the new PM’s passionate speech suggests there is now clear political will for change
For campaigners perpetually disappointed by the failure of England’s political classes to fix England’s creaking adult social care system, the fear was that Andy Burnham’s long-trailed speech on Wednesday would be less Brave New World, more Groundhog Day.
Burnham acknowledged he had been here before. Back in 2010, as health and social care secretary, he unveiled extensive proposals to overhaul social care, only for them to collapse amid rightwing media hostility and furious political rows about “death taxes”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Brave New World or Groundhog Day? Burnham revisits old ground in speech on social care

articles.author: Ben Quinn Political correspondent
articles.description:
Richard Tice had been referred to standards commissioner over undeclared sum from Farage aide George Cottrell
Parliament’s standards watchdog has declined to investigate a complaint made against Richard Tice over an undeclared loan of nearly £80,000 from Nigel Farage’s aide George Cottrell.
The Liberal Democrats had referred Reform’s deputy leader to the parliamentary standards commissioner, which was investigating Farage after the Guardian’s revelation that he received an undeclared £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Parliamentary watchdog decides against inquiry into £80,000 loan to Reform’s deputy leader

articles.author: Peter Beaumont Senior international correspondent
articles.description:
Riyadh’s decision to join US in strikes on Iran-backed militia further complicates widening and ‘unpredictable’ war

Middle East crisis – live updates

US-Saudi strikes on Iran-backed militia in Iraq have pushed the region into “uncharted territory”, analysts have warned.
Amid stark warnings of a widening and increasingly “unpredictable” conflict, Riyadh’s decision to publicly join the US in striking sites associated with Iraq’s Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), killing at least 20 fighters, has added another complicating dimension to the war.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US-Saudi strikes in Iraq push region into ‘uncharted territory’, analysts warn

articles.author: Priya Bharadia
articles.description:
Johannes Kongsnes Natland was recruited to murder unknown person by international crime gang linked to Iran
A Norwegian teenager has been found guilty of travelling to England to carry out a killing ordered by an international crime gang linked to Iran.
Johannes Kongsnes Natland, 19, from Stavanger, Norway, agreed to shoot an unknown person for €25,000 (£21,500) in March last year. Two days after he arrived in the UK armed police arrested him in a hotel room in Huddersfield, West Yorkshire, seizing two guns and ammunition.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Norwegian teenager guilty of travelling to UK to carry out contract killing

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
FSB puts Pavel Durov on international wanted lists and says his messaging app is used for sabotage and murder
Russian officials have charged Pavel Durov, the founder and chief executive of the messaging app Telegram, with aiding terrorism.
The charges against the 41-year-old Russian-born billionaire, who lives in the Gulf, are the latest step by the Kremlin to bring the internet and digital communications under its control after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Russia accuses Telegram founder of aiding terrorism in its latest online crackdown

articles.author: Tom Ambrose (now) and Taz Ali (earlier)
articles.description:
Emergency workers are continuing their search for survivors in southern Japan after yesterday’s powerful earthquake 

‘Race against time’: Japan earthquake death toll rises as rescue teams search for missing

An aerial view of a collapsed section of a bridge in the city of Yatsushiro after an earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 7.1 struck Japan’s southern Kumamoto prefecture:
Japan’s Mainichi Shimbun newspaper has been speaking to people at the Nippon Paper Industries factory in Yatsushiro, where a chimney collapsed on to the site. 

 “I never imagined something like this would happen,” said a 33-year-old man who worked at the factory. “I never thought that the chimney could collapse. I’m worried about the people inside.”

 He was off duty and at home when the earthquake struck, and was unharmed. The names of those rescued and those trapped have not yet been released. “Someone I know might be affected,” he said.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Rescue teams face ‘race against time’ in search for trapped survivors as death toll in Japan rises to at least 13 – as it happened

articles.author: Guardian staff and agencies
articles.description:
Oil price spikes after flare-up of fighting and claimed Iranian attacks on three tankers in strait of Hormuz
The US military said it knocked down an Iranian missile barrage and worked with Saudi Arabia forces to strike sites in Iraq that Tehran-backed militias have used to launch attacks in recent days. The strikes on Wednesday killed at least 20 members of a former paramilitary alliance that includes pro-Iran groups.
In what Washington cast ⁠as “an attempted surprise ⁠attack” by Tehran, Iran had launched multiple ballistic missiles at US forces in the Middle East, shattering a brief pause in fighting. Iran’s target was a US base in Jordan, Axios cited a US official as saying.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US joins forces with Saudis to strike Tehran-backed militias in Iraq

articles.author: Gavin Blair in Tokyo
articles.description:
Rescuers pulling people from the wreckage in southern Japan in a haunting repeat of disaster that struck 10 years ago

‘Race against time’: Japan earthquake death toll rises as rescue teams search for missing

“There was a voice coming from the collapsed house, and I could see a hand,” Tomohide Nagata, a volunteer firefighter, told the Kumamoto Nichinichi Shimbun. “One of our senior members crawled in and pulled him out. He was bleeding from the head, but I’m so glad he survived.”
Nagata had heard a noise coming from one completely flattened home in the rural town of Hikawa, close to the epicentre of Tuesday’s 6.8-magnitude earthquake in southern Japan. The town was one of the areas hardest hit, with numerous older houses collapsing. Terrified of the ongoing aftershocks, many residents spent Tuesday night in their cars outside Hikawa’s town hall, where staff distributed food and drinks.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘The shaking was terrifying’: stories of survival and loss emerge after Japan earthquake

articles.author: Gavin Blair in Tokyo, and Rachel Hall
articles.description:
Military mobilises thousands of personnel after quake on southern Kyushu island that registered a maximum 7 on the Japanese shindo intensity scale

Earthquake rocks southern Japanese island of Kyushu – in pictures 

At least 13 people were killed when a 6.8 magnitude earthquake struck southern Japan on Tuesday, injuring hundreds and knocking out power and water to tens of thousands.
“There are people who are still waiting to be rescued, and it’s a race against time,” the prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, said on Wednesday. “We will go all out to find and rescue as many people as we can.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Race against time’: Japan earthquake death toll rises as rescue teams search for missing

articles.author: Guardian staff and agencies
articles.description:
Potential toxic substance detected in several of 15 elephants found dead in Kenya’s Amboseli national park

Officials are investigating the deaths of 15 elephants over the past month in Kenya’s Amboseli national park.
The Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) said 10 of the elephants showed signs of partial paralysis before dying within two days.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Kenya investigating unexpected deaths of 15 elephants in national park

articles.author: Dara Kerr and agencies
articles.description:
Move comes as the Trump administration has increasingly sought to keep Chinese technology out of the US
The Federal Communications Commission announced a ban on humanoid robots from China on Tuesday, saying that the technology poses “unacceptable risks” to the country’s national security. The move comes as the Trump administration has increasingly sought to keep Chinese technology out of the US.
The FCC defines the banned robots as “advanced robotic devices”, which include humanoids and animal-like quadrupeds.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US bans humanoid robots from China, citing ‘unacceptable risks’

articles.author: Olivia Bowden in Toronto
articles.description:
Data shows Canadians have replaced US vacations with other international trips in apparent rebuke to Trump
Canadians spent $3.3bn less on travel to the US in 2025 than in the previous year, as Donald Trump’s hostile policies towards his northern neighbour continue to incur an economic cost, new government data shows.
The research also indicates that Canadians are not bucking travel overall and instead have replaced US vacations with other international destinations, in a rebuke to Trump’s tariff regime and the president’s continued musings on annexing Canada.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Canadians spent $3.3bn less on travel to US in 2025 after Trump’s return to office

articles.author: Shah Meer Baloch in Islamabad
articles.description:
Local civil rights group alleges authorities removed evidence of killings amid communications blackout
At least 30 people are alleged to have been killed in Pakistan-administered Kashmir in the past two days as part of what has been claimed is a brutal state crackdown that has engulfed the disputed region for weeks.
According to a local civil society group, Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC), the Pakistani security services fired on tens of thousands of peaceful protesters, killing 25 people on Monday and five more on Tuesday.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Pakistan accused of fatally shooting 30 unarmed protesters in Kashmir

articles.author: Oliver Milman
articles.description:
Three years after Maui wildfires many still struggle with ‘biological, emotional and social consequences’, study says
A spate of ferocious wildfires across North America and Europe, worsened by the climate crisis, has incinerated homes and forests and forced thousands of people to flee. Previous fires suggest the effects of these blazes may linger for years to come.
The current fires and their plumes of smoke can appear to be a temporary, if immediate, crisis. Nearly 1,000 fires have sprung into life in the boreal forests of Canada, causing the evacuation of towns and toxic smoke to waft into major Canadian and US cities, prompting threats of retribution from Donald Trump, who bizarrely accused Canada of “poisoning” his country’s air.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Past fires suggest effects of Europe and North America wildfires may linger for years

articles.author: Deepa Parent
articles.description:
At least 1,500 protest after six men on drug-related charges put in solitary confinement before possible execution
Prisoners at Iran’s largest jail have sewn their lips shut as hundreds of them joined a mass hunger strike amid a surge in executions over drug offences and charges linked to anti-government protests.
The hunger strike, involving at least 1,500 death row prisoners at Ghezel Hesar prison near Tehran, began two weeks ago after six men convicted on drug-related charges were transferred to solitary confinement before their possible execution, according to Iranian rights groups.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Prisoners at Iran’s largest jail sew lips shut in hunger strike as executions soar

articles.author: Facundo Iglesia in Buenos Aires and Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro
articles.description:
President also blames Brazil and Mexico and says online critics ‘do not want the ideas of freedom to succeed’
More than a week has passed since Ferran Torres scored the extra-time goal that gave Spain its second World Cup, but – at least for Argentina’s president – the tournament is not over.
Javier Milei has claimed that a coordinated “anti-Argentina campaign” was behind criticism of the country’s team, accusations of racism among its fans and conspiracy theories alleging that Lionel Messi’s side was secretly being favoured by Fifa.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Javier Milei accuses US Democrats of financing ‘anti-Argentina campaign’ at World Cup

articles.author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi
articles.description:
Cockroach Janta party says government has broken promise, with detentions in Delhi, Assam, West Bengal and Bihar
India’s youth-led “Cockroach” movement, whose nationwide protests forced the resignation of the education minister, has accused the government of backtracking on its promise not to act against student protesters and has threatened to restart demonstrations.
The Cockroach Janta party (CJP), which organised mass protests over exam paper leaks and other irregularities, said it had received reports of hundreds of students being detained or “harassed” by police.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: India’s Cockroach movement threatens to restart protests after mass student arrests

articles.author: William Christou in Zefta; photographs by Oliver Marsden
articles.description:
In normal times the Mashala shelter founder takes in strays, but in wartime, he is the only lifeline for animals in the area
During Israel’s 2006 war against Hezbollah, Houssein Hamze woke up one night to the sound of barking. Alarmed, he got up to check on the dog – his first rescue pet. Moments later, a bomb dropped next to his home and a piece of shrapnel landed right where he had been sleeping.
“I swear to God, he really saved me from death. Animals always possess a sixth sense we don’t have,” Hamze said.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: A dog saved Houssein Hamze from a bomb. When war returned, he stayed to care for Lebanon’s animals

articles.author: John Bartlett in Santiago
articles.description:
Nelson Haase Mazzei was sentenced for murdering Jara in 2023, but fled from authorities in Chile
More than 50 years after the murder of the Chilean folk singer Víctor Jara, the last man wanted in connection with his death has been tracked down and brought to justice.
Nelson Haase Mazzei, a retired colonel, fled from authorities in 2023 after he and six other retired soldiers were sentenced in absentia for murdering Jara and another man.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Pinochet-era soldier jailed for killing folk singer Víctor Jara 53 years ago

articles.author: Agence France-Press in Montreal
articles.description:
No one was injured and no suspects have been identified in connection to shooting near Toronto compound, police say
Shots were fired near the US consulate in Toronto early on Monday but no one was injured in the second shooting near the diplomatic compound in four months.
“Officers heard a firearm being discharged in the area,” and “a white sedan was seen fleeing the scene”, Toronto police said on X.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Shots fired near US consulate in Canada for second time in four months

articles.author: Brendan Wood for MetDesk
articles.description:
Wind and record-breaking heat are fuelling the continent’s explosive fire season, with Spain and France among worst hit

Explainer: what is a ‘fire cloud’, and how have they worsened wildfires in Europe?

Europe wildfires live – latest updates

A combination of an unusually wet winter, very low rainfall since spring and repeated record-breaking summer heatwaves is likely to explain why wildfires have ignited, spread and resisted control so readily across France and Spain in recent days.
About 90% of wildfires are started by human activity, typically igniting “fine fuels” such as vegetation grass, pine needles, litter and twigs. And recent weather has almost certainly made ignition far easier. Drought in western Europe has turned this vegetation – which normally dries after only a few hours of heat and low rainfall – into tinder.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Weather tracker: Why Europe’s wildfires are proving so fierce and difficult to stop

articles.author: Samuel Okiror
articles.description:
Government move follows months of drought and crop failures in Karamoja, with 1.5m people facing malnutrition
Uganda has launched emergency food relief distribution after at least 19 deaths from hunger were reported in an area of prolonged drought in the east of the country.
A crisis has been building in the Karamoja region of Uganda as crops have failed without the season’s expected rains, leaving the region’s 1.5 million people facing acute food shortages and rising malnutrition.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Uganda begins emergency food handouts after 19 die from hunger

articles.author: Hettie O'Brien
articles.description:
In today’s newsletter: Across ​the country, a ​younger generation is turning private disillusionment into public defiance​ against a government that once felt untouchable
Good morning. As flames engulfed parts of France and Spain this weekend, in India, the prime minister, Narendra Modi, was trying to put out a very different kind of fire. Thousands of people arrived in Delhi on Saturday to demand the resignation of his education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan. When he stepped down in the early afternoon, the protests turned into a triumphant block party.
But the Cockroach protests that have swept through India this summer are about much more than a single minister. They have humiliated Modi and undermined the indomitable power of his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) that has ruled India for the…
articles.title: Monday briefing: ​How the Cockroach ​protests ​have expose​d the ​cracks in ​India’s government

articles.author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi
articles.description:
Ally forced to resign, with opposition parties reinvigorated and strongman leader’s grip over media channels rocked
Even the night before Narendra Modi accepted the resignation of his education minister, India’s prime minister appeared confident that the largest mass uprising to take place in his 12 years in power would do little to rattle his government.
Addressing his “young friends” in a late-night Instagram selfie reel on Friday, he thanked the people – who were mobilised en masse across the country, shouting anti-government slogans – for their “thoughtful suggestions”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: India’s Cockroach Janta party protest victory signals trouble ahead for Modi

articles.author: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg and agencies
articles.description:
The men were convicted over alleged plan to stage coup and organise deadly demonstrations over fuel prices last year
Two Russian men have been found guilty by an Angolan court of terrorism and spying after being accused of planning a coup and helping to organise deadly demonstrations in the southern African country last year.
Lev Lakshtanov and Igor Ratchin were sentenced to eight and 11 years in jail respectively. They had denied the charges, claiming they were in Angola for cultural and business activities.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Two Russian men jailed in Angola for terrorism and spying

articles.author: Hannah Al-Othman North of England correspondent
articles.description:
September exercise called off after Kenya raises concerns over funding and jurisdiction for criminal offences
The British army has been forced to cancel training for its troops in Kenya after the Kenyan government refused to ratify a bilateral defence agreement.
While the UK government wanted to renew the existing agreement, Kenyan lawmakers had sought changes to give local authorities greater powers to hold British soldiers accountable for any offences committed in the country.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: MoD cancels army training in Kenya over powers to prosecute British soldiers

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
UK resident was evacuated from Democratic Republic of the Congo where there is an outbreak of the disease
A humanitarian worker is being monitored at a specialist hospital in London after potential exposure to the Ebola virus.
The UK resident was medically evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) where the worker had been treating patients with the disease, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Health worker monitored for Ebola in London hospital after working in DRC

articles.author: Robert Mackey, Lucy Campbell, Jo Walters, Rachel Leingang and Tom Ambrose
articles.description:
This blog is now closed. You can read our latest story here

Sign up for US Breaking News email

Gary Peters, the Democratic ranking member on the homeland security committee, said that the committee has a long history of bipartisan inquiry and oversight, and the subject matter of risky research and the origins of covid-19 are a legitimate area to study.
But today’s hearing with Anthony Fauci was not an example of that, Peters said.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Senate committee delays vote on Todd Blanche attorney general nomination – as it happened

articles.author: Sam Levine
articles.description:
Republican John Cornyn says he will not back nomination without written confirmation $1.8bn slush fund is dead
Todd Blanche’s hopes of becoming US attorney general seemed to be in jeopardy on Wednesday after the Department of Justice did not provide written assurances to a key Republican senator that a $1.8bn slush fund was dead.
The US Senate judiciary committee postponed a vote scheduled for Thursday on whether to advance Blanche’s nomination.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump’s pick for US attorney general Todd Blanche in jeopardy as vote postponed

articles.author: Anna Betts
articles.description:
Longtime Epstein associate serving 20-year sentence for sex-trafficking crimes has exhausted series of appeals 
The US Senate on Wednesday unanimously passed a resolution declaring its opposition to any presidential pardon for Ghislaine Maxwell, the longtime Jeffrey Epstein associate who is currently serving a 20-year prison sentence for sex-trafficking crimes.
Introduced by Senator Jacky Rosen, a Democrat of Nevada, the resolution states that Maxwell “should not be granted a Presidential pardon or any form of clemency for her crimes with Jeffrey Epstein relating to the sexual exploitation and abuse of minors”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Senate unanimously passes resolution opposing pardon for Ghislaine Maxwell

articles.author: Gaya Gupta
articles.description:
Rates remain unchanged for fifth time since December as tenuous Iran peace deal pushes energy prices up again
The US Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday in a divided vote, indicating growing pressure on the central bank to address heightened inflation.
The Fed’s federal open market committee voted 9-3 to maintain rates, with three dissenting members indicating a preference to raise the rate by a quarter-percentage point. It was the first time in a decade that three board members shared dissent over a policy decision.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Fed holds interest rates steady despite Trump’s renewed calls to lower them

articles.author: Joseph Gedeon in Washington
articles.description:
Planned overhaul forms part of president’s broader pattern of directing changes in Washington after arch and ballroom
Donald Trump announced on Wednesday a $22bn plan to rebuild Washington’s Dulles international airport on Wednesday after the US president personally weighed in on the design of the capital’s main international gateway.
“In the end, you can end up with – I think – maybe the best airport, and one of the biggest airports, anywhere in the world, and it’s going to be a great thing for Washington DC,” the president said during an announcement at the Oval Office on Wednesday.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump announces $22bn plan to rebuild Dulles international airport

articles.author: Matt Gurney
articles.description:
The White House fails to understand that Mark Carney and Canada’s regional leaders can’t cave in to the US president: it’s too toxic to voters
• Matt Gurney is a journalist based in Toronto
Though many hate to admit it, Canadians have long wished for more attention from the US. Well, we’re getting it now. And it turns out that President Trump and some of his top supporters in the Maga movement don’t much like us.
The first big hint was when he started talking about annexing us, saying we couldn’t survive without American support. But the most recent example of Trump’s dislike for Canada can be seen in his latest tariff policies. Canada was largely spared the impact of his “Liberation Day” tariffs in April 2025 by its pre-existing free trade deal with the US (and Mexico), but earlier this month, as expected, the US declined to extend that deal for another 16-year term. It’s now subject to annual renegotiations. Then, last week, the White House announced tariffs as high as 50% on a selection of Canadian products including, for the first time, items previously protected by the trade agreement. The US called it retaliation for Canadian trade practices.
Matt Gurney is a journalist based in Toronto, and co-editor of The Line, an online magazine
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump has singled out us Canadians for special treatment in his tariff war – there is no choice but to get nasty | Matt Gurney

articles.author: Arwa Mahdawi
articles.description:
The US vice-president is facing a barrage of allegations and complaints from inside and outside the Republican ranks. Good news for Marco Rubio – but not for the rest of the world
There’s something a bit off about JD Vance. And I mean that literally: the vice-president has been snacking on sauerkraut and other fermented foods as part of a weight-loss regime. Health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr got a number of Trump officials, including Vance, on to the diet, and is thrilled with the results. “Within 20 days I lost 20 pounds,” Kennedy said at an event in Michigan last month. “JD Vance is also on the diet and you can see how different he looks.” Dunno about that: still looks like a naked opportunist to me.
If you want to get into Donald Trump’s good books, improving your looks is a surefire way to do so. According to MS Now, the president is loving Vance’s svelte new figure; it’s helped propel him back into Trump’s good graces. Which is lucky for him because he doesn’t have many other fans. They may be full of beneficial bacteria, but everyone around Vance seems to hate his guts.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Even Maga is falling out of love with JD Vance. If only his rivals weren’t even worse … | Arwa Mahdawi

articles.author: Arwa Mahdawi
articles.description:
Is it normal for a sitting senator to have to routinely submit proofs of life to a public who suspect he might be braindead? Just asking for 340 million friends 
Is it normal for a sitting senator to have to routinely submit proofs of life to a public who suspect he might be braindead? Just asking for 340 million friends in the US. Mitch McConnell was hospitalized for a medical event on 14 June and we are now in week six of What on Earth Is Going on With Mitch? – a mystery that has riveted the nation.
According to McConnell’s team there isn’t actually a mystery at all. The 84-year-old is doing great, they want us to know. So great that they have now released two photos to prove it.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Welcome to America, where you’re never quite sure if your senator is dead or not | Arwa Mahdawi

articles.author: Arwa Mahdawi
articles.description:
The 20-year-old crypto bro likes to keep a low profile. He could still be forced to testify before the House oversight committee
Unlike his garrulous father, Barron Trump seems to be a man of few words. The president’s youngest son has been busy flogging energy drinks and making millions from cryptocurrency schemes, but he’s not big on public speaking. Indeed, the best-known clip of him talking is probably from when he was four years old and said “I like my suitcase” in a Slovenian accent.
Still, while 20-year-old Barron Trump might prefer to stay behind the scenes, he may find himself hauled in front of Congress and forced to answer some difficult questions. Last week, Yassamin Ansari, a Democratic congresswoman and a member of the House oversight committee, called for Barron to testify about his alleged connections to the toxic influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate. The Tate brothers, who have become household names by monetising misogyny, were recently arrested in Miami, just before Andrew was due to co-host a bare-knuckle boxing event. They’re now fighting extradition to the UK, and face allegations of rape, assault, trafficking and offences relating to “indecent images of a child and extreme pornography”. They deny these charges.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How close is the Trump administration to the toxic Tate brothers? Let’s ask the president’s son Barron … | Arwa Mahdawi

articles.author: Owen Myers
articles.description:
The comedian and actor’s new Netflix special is a gleefully absurd take on politics and potty-mouthed humor
Mary Beth Barone knows exactly who will be offended by her new Netflix special. “JK Rowling, Republicans, establishment Democrats, the British, the Irish and Zionists,” she tells me, reading a list from her Notes app. Then there’s “Katy Kats – which is what Katy Perry calls her fans – and male comedians and one specific girl named Tatiana”. When informed that this encompasses over half of the population of the US, she beams.
Barone’s comedy is a delicate balance between sweetness and cynicism. In her standup she’ll adopt a ditzy pose while she tears down morally bankrupt politicians, sends up cis male entitlement or implores her audience to have sex with moderates in the hope of bringing them over to the left. In the past five years, she has edged her way closer to the mainstream with a Comedy Central web-series, a couple of standup spots on Jimmy Fallon’s late-night show, and a podcast co-hosted with her friend Benito Skinner that is so popular it has its own merch line. The past 12 months have seen her career go into overdrive: now she is the co-lead of a wildly popular TV show (Overcompensating, created by Skinner), chats to the A-list on the Golden Globes’ red carpet and sits front row at New York fashion week.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Mary Beth Barone on provocative jokes, Palestine and manosphere misogyny: ‘It’s hard to stomach that those are my co-workers’

articles.author: George Chidi in Marietta, Georgia, Shrai Popat in North York, Maine, Rachel Leingang in Superior, Wisconsin, and Joseph Gedeon in Washington. Graphics by Andrew Witherspoon
articles.description:
Whether in favor of or against the US-Israel war on Iran, people across the country are left holding the bill and wondering on its purpose
Five months after the United States and Israel started a historically unpopular war against Iran that was going to supposedly last weeks, the fighting has refused to resolve in victory, defeat or peace. Iran’s supreme leader had been killed in the opening strikes, ceasefires broke down, and the strait of Hormuz has been closed and reopened.
For voters interviewed across the country, while the damage may be distant, the residual effects have shown up at the pump, on the grocery bill and in a phone call telling a spouse they have a day to report for deployment. And for a country still absorbing the aftermath of Israel’s war on Gaza – funded to the tune of billions of dollars by the United States – the war in Iran lands on top of an already raw argument about what American power is for.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Americans feel pinch of continued Iran war: ‘It’s screwed everything up’

articles.author: Richard Luscombe
articles.description:
Astronauts for America liken effort to instill trust and faith back in constitution’s principles and democratic institutions to ‘making a course correction’
Orbiting 250 miles above the US in the international space station, astronaut Cady Coleman did not look down and see red or blue states, sanctuary cities or communities occupied by thousands of federal immigration enforcement agents in camouflage uniforms and automatic weapons.
What she saw was a single land, from Pacific to Atlantic, no borders or partitions, just a united America, and a population valuing its equality while convinced that what brought them together was far greater than anything that divided them.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Our country is the mission’: more than 100 ex-Nasa astronauts launch new voting campaign

articles.author: Hilary Beaumont in San Bernardino, California
articles.description:
After masked agents fired on his truck, Francisco Longoria was ambushed, charged and jailed – only for the case against him to fall apart. Now he and his family are seeking justice, and says the harrowing experience is part of a troubling pattern
It was just after 8am on 16 August and Francisco Longoria, who runs a party supply business, was driving his truck down a suburban southern California street to deliver a jumper for a water slide. But this ordinary Saturday morning turned into a nightmare when, suddenly, three unmarked vehicles stopped his truck and four masked men jumped out.
Longoria, who had brought his son Jonathan Longoria and son-in-law Daniel Rascon with him, wondered if they were being abducted.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: He was shot at by ICE, then wrongfully accused. His nightmare had only just begun

articles.author: Hosted by Kai Wright and Carter Sherman , with David Smith and Rachel Leingang . Produced by Suzanne Gaber and Tiara Chiaramonte , edited by Anabel Bacon , engineered by Ivan Kuraev
articles.description:
Earlier this year, Congress reached a depressing milestone: 86% of Americans, a record high, disapproved of its job performance. But this summer, there have been some signs that shifts are underway. On the left, House Democrats have just voted in unprecedented numbers to withhold military aid from Israel, and across the country, progressive candidates are running competitive primary campaigns that are energizing a base fed up with the status quo. On the right, Republicans are reeling from the sudden death of Lindsey Graham, the South Carolina senator and one of Donald Trump's staunchest supporters. Mitch McConnell, the former Senate majority leader, remains sequestered following a health scare in June, raising questions of if a changing of the guard might be underway there, too. Kai Wright and Carter Sherman are joined by David Smith, the Guardian's Washington bureau chief and Rachel Leingang, midwest political correspondent, to discuss gerontocracy, transparency, the rise of the Democratic Socialists of America and just how much of an inflection point this summer might be for both parties


This page was amended on 23 July 2026. A previous version misspelled Lindsey Graham. 

 Continue reading...
articles.title: Is US Congress finally on the verge of a change? – Stateside with Kai and Carter

articles.author: Sam Levine Zhara Keogh Michael Kalenderian Sarah Bertram
articles.description:
Donald Trump delivered a primetime address to the country on Thursday, claiming that declassified intelligence showed Chinese interference in US elections. The US president revived long-running attacks on election security, despite a US intelligence assessment that found no evidence Beijing altered the 2020 vote, which he lost. The Guardian's voting rights reporter Sam Levine factchecks some of Trump's claims

Trump is invoking foreign election interference to justify his own - Opinion

 Continue reading...
articles.title: Fact-checking Donald Trump’s address on Chinese election interference – video

articles.author: Hosted by Jonathan Freedland . Produced by May Robson, Jacob Liebenberg, Ned Carter Miles and the executive producer is Maz Ebtehaj .
articles.description:
The debate about how old is too old to serve in public office has resurfaced this week after the shock death of the Republican senator Lindsey Graham and the surprise return of Mitch McConnell, the 84-year-old senator who published a photo of himself in hospital after a long absence from the spotlight.
With rumours continuing to swirl around Donald Trump’s health, why is it US politicians seem to cling on to power for so long?
Jonathan Freedland speaks to Alexis Coe, a presidential historian and columnist for the New York Times Book review, about whether the US is becoming a gerontocracy – and what can be done about it
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Are American politicians too old? | Politics Weekly America

articles.author: Hosted by Kai Wright and Carter Sherman , with Shrai Popat and Lauren Gambino . Produced by Meg Driscoll, edited by Anabel Bacon , engineered by Ivan Kuraev
articles.description:
Earlier this week, Graham Platner, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Maine, was accused by a former partner of sexual assault. Platner denies the allegations, but on Wednesday, he suspended his campaign, accusing the “political establishment” of tanking his candidacy. But this is only the most recent scandal to have surfaced around Platner’s campaign — over the past year, the oyster farmer and combat veteran was revealed to have a tattoo that closely resembled a Totenkopf (a widely recognized Nazi symbol), a long paper trail of racist, misogynist and homophobic posts on Reddit, and in June, the New York Times published allegations from three former partners about Platner’s “toxic” behavior in their relationships, including, in several cases, physical intimidation (allegations Platner denied).
As Democrats regroup and evaluate their dwindling chances to flip the Senate in November, hosts Kai Wright and Carter Sherman are joined by Guardian political reporters Lauren Gambino and Shrai Popat to ask why voters flocked to Platner, why they were reluctant to abandon him as the scandals came out — and what the whole mess says about who gets the privilege of political redemption.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Why Graham Platner wasn’t the answer to the Democrats’ man problem – Stateside with Kai and Carter

articles.author: Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor
articles.description:
Prime minister to highlight investment in communities as he launches next phase of nuclear submarine replacement
Andy Burnham will place the renewal of Trident at the heart of his vision of a reindustrialised Britain on Thursday when he travels to Barrow-in-Furness to launch the next phase of the nuclear submarine replacement programme.
The new prime minister intends to emphasise that defence spending on projects such as the £31bn Dreadnought-class boats built in the Cumbrian town is a case study of taxpayer investment revitalising communities around the UK.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trident renewal central to defence spending, says Andy Burnham

articles.author: Helena Smith in Athens
articles.description:
Greek authorities identify remains as those of Elizabeth Jane Ross after discovery in a derelict building 11 days ago 
A body found in a suitcase in an abandoned building in central Athens has been identified as that of a 38-year-old British woman.
Eleven days after the find, and following an appeal to foreign law enforcement agencies, Greek police shed some light on the mystery of the body that until Wednesday had remained unidentified.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Body found in suitcase in Athens is that of 38-year-old British woman

articles.author: Aletha Adu Political correspondent
articles.description:
Scotland Yard says threshold not met for criminal action against Green leader, who has refused to apologise to his Reform rival
No further action will be taken by police after Zack Polanski shared a photo of a man with a T-shirt showing a guillotine and the phrase “we’re only making plans for Nigel”.
The Metropolitan police’s decision comes after the Green party leader for England and Wales said he had made an “inadvertent mistake” and would not apologise to Nigel Farage.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Police take no further action over Polanski sharing Farage guillotine image

articles.author: Dan Milmo and Vikram Dodd
articles.description:
Details of parents and staff, including email addresses and phone numbers, are among data taken by cybercriminals
The Department for Education and a police database have been targeted by a cyber-attack, exposing more than 740,000 pieces of data.
Details of government officials, senior school leaders, university staff, police officers and members of the public have been taken by hackers.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Hackers steal sensitive data from UK Department for Education and police

articles.author: Patrick Butler Social policy editor
articles.description:
Rightwing media hostility helped sink his reform plans in 2010, but the new PM’s passionate speech suggests there is now clear political will for change
For campaigners perpetually disappointed by the failure of England’s political classes to fix England’s creaking adult social care system, the fear was that Andy Burnham’s long-trailed speech on Wednesday would be less Brave New World, more Groundhog Day.
Burnham acknowledged he had been here before. Back in 2010, as health and social care secretary, he unveiled extensive proposals to overhaul social care, only for them to collapse amid rightwing media hostility and furious political rows about “death taxes”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Brave New World or Groundhog Day? Burnham revisits old ground in speech on social care

articles.author: Ben Quinn Political correspondent
articles.description:
Richard Tice had been referred to standards commissioner over undeclared sum from Farage aide George Cottrell
Parliament’s standards watchdog has declined to investigate a complaint made against Richard Tice over an undeclared loan of nearly £80,000 from Nigel Farage’s aide George Cottrell.
The Liberal Democrats had referred Reform’s deputy leader to the parliamentary standards commissioner, which was investigating Farage after the Guardian’s revelation that he received an undeclared £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Parliamentary watchdog decides against inquiry into £80,000 loan to Reform’s deputy leader

articles.author: Gwyn Topham Transport correspondent
articles.description:
Transport for London claims polluting diesel vehicles had been able to enter clean air zone without having to pay
Transport for London is pursuing a potential £1bn legal action against car manufacturers over vehicles that it argues should not have been allowed to drive freely in the capital’s clean-air zone.
The high court heard that TfL was making allegations of “fraud and negligence” against manufacturers including Stellantis, Jaguar Land Rover, BMW and Nissan over their vehicles’ levels of diesel emissions.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: TfL brings case worth up to £1bn against carmakers over Ulez compliance

articles.author: Priya Bharadia
articles.description:
Johannes Kongsnes Natland was recruited to murder unknown person by international crime gang linked to Iran
A Norwegian teenager has been found guilty of travelling to England to carry out a killing ordered by an international crime gang linked to Iran.
Johannes Kongsnes Natland, 19, from Stavanger, Norway, agreed to shoot an unknown person for €25,000 (£21,500) in March last year. Two days after he arrived in the UK armed police arrested him in a hotel room in Huddersfield, West Yorkshire, seizing two guns and ammunition.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Norwegian teenager guilty of travelling to UK to carry out contract killing

articles.author: Nadia Khomami Arts and culture correspondent
articles.description:
V&A Storehouse dispute centres on toilet and hydration breaks as employees across V&A in London also vote to strike in wider action
Staff at the V&A’s Storehouse site in east London have voted overwhelmingly to strike in a dispute over what they say are inadequate toilet and hydration breaks.
They will join staff across V&A sites in London who on Wednesday also voted to strike in a wider dispute over pay, working conditions, and the museum having declined to seek living wage accreditation.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Staff at newest V&A site in London vote overwhelmingly for strike action

articles.author: Andrew Sparrow
articles.description:
The prime minister says that current inefficiencies in the system will be tackled first, as he reveals final recommendations will be out by summer 2027
Andy Burnham is speaking now.
In a reference to how he started campaing for social care reform almost two decades ago, he says it is good to see faces in the room “who’ve been on this journey with me for a long, a long time”.
When someone in your family is receiving care, you look at everything through new eyes, don’t you? You notice things that maybe you didn’t notice before because you watch it so closely and so carefully.
And I’ve just been really overwhelmed by their care, the skill in what they do, the professionalism.
Can I just remind everybody that nobody thought we could get everybody in off the streets?
So we can do difficult in this country and we can do it well.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK politics: Burnham does not rule out tax rises for social care reform – as it happened

articles.author: Anna Isaac City editor
articles.description:
Exclusive: Sources say Fiona Cottrell told bankers the transfers, received 24-72 hours before her donations to Reform, came from her son
The convicted fraudster George Cottrell transferred a total of more than $2m to his mother, Fiona Cottrell, in the days before her 2024 donations to Reform UK, the Guardian understands.
Financial industry sources told the Guardian that Fiona received one deposit of $1.4m and two tranches of more than $300,000 each – money she attributed to having come from her son, George, when bankers asked about the deposits.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Revealed: George Cottrell transferred $2m to his mother days before her donations to Reform UK

articles.author: Joanna Partridge
articles.description:
Strong corporate results buoy market as investors move money away from tech and semiconductor stocks 
London’s FTSE 100 stock index has touched a fresh high, driven by strong corporate results as investors moved money away from tech and semiconductor stocks amid the global tech stock sell-off.
The UK’s blue chip index rose as high as 10,951 points on Wednesday morning before falling back slightly, its best level since 27 February, the day before the US and Israel began attacks on Iran and sparked stock market volatility.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: FTSE 100 hits record high despite AI sell-off

articles.author: Presented by Reged Ahmad with Ben Smee. Produced by Miles Herbert with sound design by Lu Hill. The executive producer is Hannah Parkes
articles.description:
Twenty-five years ago, on a desolate stretch of Australian highway, Bradley John Murdoch flagged down British backpackers Joanne Lees and Peter Falconio. Falconio was never seen again.
Now, as police continue to try to bring closure for his family, one former British government expert says he knows the ‘most likely’ place where Falconio’s body was hidden
Queensland correspondent Ben Smee joins Reged Ahmad as police try to finally close the case on the murder of Peter Falconio
Read more:
Peter Falconio murder: British expert says he has identified a ‘most likely’ burial location
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Will we ever find Peter Falconio’s body? - podcast

articles.author: Mark Brown North of England correspondent; photographs by Gary Calton
articles.description:
Laughter, disbelief and outrage over video appearing to show Saltburn player tricking umpire into giving batters out
At the Saltburn over-60s ukulele club there was a unanimous reaction to news that the town’s cricket club were being compared to the Argentina football team: laughter. Then a spirited rendition of I Love to Boogie.
On the seafront, a litter-picking volunteer was looking forward to the Wednesday night quiz just to get the gossip. But she had her own view. “All I would say is it’s just not cricket, is it?”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Saltburn are the Argentina of local cricket’: victims and neighbours on the ‘Clicky Ponting’ scandal

articles.author: Alexandra Topping
articles.description:
Exclusive: The former education secretary on her new role as Labour chair and continuing as the minister for women and equalities
If Bridget Phillipson is angry at losing a job – one that, in the brief honeymoon period at the start of Keir Starmer’s Labour government, she called the “honour of my life” – she is doing a good job of hiding it. “It hurts to lose a job you love,” she says. “Being education secretary was amazing … and I’m really proud of what we achieved in that time.”
Phillipson was removed during the clearout of Starmer’s cabinet when Andy Burnham took office last week, and was replaced by Lucy Powell, an ally of the new prime minister. But unlike some spurned colleagues, Phillipson didn’t walk away from government, instead accepting the brief of women and equalities minister – now a cabinet standalone position – which she had previously held alongside education.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘It hurts to lose a job you love’: Starmer loyalist Bridget Phillipson fights on despite cabinet demotion

articles.author: Nadia Khomami Arts and culture correspondent
articles.description:
Actor and musician responds hours after BBC documentary airs claims by four women that allegedly took place when he was in 30s and 40s
The actor and singer Jared Leto has denied accusations of criminal sexual conduct made by four women in a BBC documentary, with the alleged offences taking place when the women were teenagers.
The incidents reported by the BBC are alleged to have taken place between 2002 and 2016, when the actor was in his 30s and 40s. He is now 54.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Jared Leto denies accusations of criminal sexual conduct against teenagers

articles.author: Pippa Neill
articles.description:
Environment Agency names seven regions affected by unusually hot and dry weather and shortage of water
Half of England is officially in drought, with July set to be the driest on record after winter floods, the Environment Agency has said.
The “flash drought” developed quickly because of unusually low rainfall and high temperatures.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Half of England officially in ‘exceptionally serious’ drought

articles.author: Helena Horton
articles.description:
Exclusive: British garden staple becomes plant most frequently reported as suffering in heat, charity reports
With their lush foliage and blooms that turn pink, purple or blue depending on the soil, hydrangeas are a firm favourite in Britain.
The shrubs bloom throughout summer and have historically thrived in the mild, damp British climate. But hotter summers and heatwaves such as the one hitting parts of England this week are putting the flower at risk in the south of the country, the Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) has said.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Hotter summers may force RHS to move hydrangeas to north of England

articles.author: Joanna Partridge and Sarah Butler
articles.description:
Rise to £1.1bn in first six months of year for bakery chain largely down to opening of new stores

Business live – latest updates

Iced matcha lattes and a bigger range of salads and chicken rolls helped Greggs to boost its sales during the string of summer heatwaves, as the bakery said it was adapting to the UK’s increasingly hot summers.
Total sales at Britain’s biggest fast food business rose to £1.1bn for the first six months of the year, 7.2% higher than the same period a year earlier.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Greggs sales jump as iced matcha lattes and chicken rolls become heatwave hits

articles.author: Gwyn Topham and agencies
articles.description:
CAA says airport can recoup £320m through higher airline charges, which are usually passed on to travellers
Heathrow passengers face decades of higher fares after the regulator overrode airline objections to allow the airport to charge for planning work to build its proposed third runway.
The Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) said it had permitted Heathrow Airport Limited (HAL) to recover early costs of up to £320m spent on developing its expansion plan since 2025.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Heathrow passengers face higher fares as airport can recover early expansion plan costs

articles.author: Louisa Loveluck and Harry Davies
articles.description:
Experts say lower-severity charges for American service personnel are deepening traumatic impact on survivors
American service personnel accused of rape on British soil are being charged with lesser offences by their military courts, a discrepancy that experts say is deepening the traumatic impact on survivors long after verdicts are passed.
There are more than 12,000 personnel stationed in US military bases across the UK, most of them in England. Although UK law enforcement has primary jurisdiction over crimes that occur when personnel are off duty, local police often choose to cede authority to the American military.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Why US military prosecutes alleged rapes of women in UK as ‘sexual assaults’

articles.author: Dan Milmo
articles.description:
Energy regulator’s plan would mean upfront fees or financial security via letters of credit, bonds or cash deposits
Datacentre projects in Britain will be forced to pay hundreds of millions of pounds to plug into the power grid under proposals to tackle a growing electricity connection logjam.
Ofgem, the sector watchdog, said it was taking action to discourage “speculative” datacentre projects from causing unnecessary delays to the grid connection queue, which includes hospitals, schools and housing developments.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Datacentre projects face fees for grid access to ease connection queue, Ofgem says

articles.author: Sally Weale Education correspondent
articles.description:

articles.author: Tim Burrows. Photographs by Andy Hall
articles.description:
Nigel Farage’s constituency takes in genteel resorts and one of England’s poorest villages. With a snap byelection approaching, what do the residents want from the Reform UK leader – or the bin who’s challenging him?
‘If it’s the Tin Man, then I suppose I’ll vote for Nigel,” says a Clacton resident, a retiree on a slow stroll towards the seafront, when I ask whom she will vote for in the forthcoming byelection. “I would sooner have Farage than the Tin Man!” As political slogans go, it is as good as any.
The sun is beating down, but the sky is hazy, which accurately describes the mood of this constituency since the Reform UK leader quit as MP for Clacton on 7 July, forcing a byelection that sent shock waves through Westminster and confusion through Clacton. I am spending a couple of days here with the photographer Andy Hall, traversing the coast between Jaywick to the west and Walton-on-the-Naze to the east. An incessant wind is blowing from the North Sea, sending waves crashing on to Clacton beach. Nicky Friday, who at 11am is already handing out 99s from her aptly named kiosk, Seabreeze, isn’t exactly exercised by the Reform UK leader’s latest gambit. “This is going to sound terrible, but I’m so busy running this business and working here,” she says. “I don’t really do politics.”
Nicky Friday, who owns and runs the Seabreeze kiosk in Clacton

On a chilly day in December 1945, Bernard Lovell, a physicist at the University of Manchester, struck out for the Cheshire countryside to study cosmic rays, the streams of high-energy particles that crisscross the universe. Peering at the signals from his army surplus radar, he made an unexpected discovery: radio reflections from the ionised trails of shooting stars.
The work marked the birth of radio astronomy at Jodrell Bank. A year later, engineers at the site mounted a radar on the base of a searchlight, providing sweeping access to speeding meteors. When Sputnik launched in 1957, they had just completed the Lovell telescope, the largest radio telescope in the world, the only one capable of tracking the Soviet satellite.

articles.description:
James Cameron’s high-octane film sequel is a blueprint for modern action space slashers
• Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
It is difficult to believe that James Cameron’s Aliens was released into cinemas 40 years ago. The seminal space shooter took the original Alien – a tense slasher film with a tiny cast and one monster – and transformed it into an intergalactic war movie crammed with wry one-liners, massive guns and an actual boss battle finale. As a 14-year-old, I stood in line at the Tatton Gatley cinema, unsure if I’d be allowed in – I came out three hours later a changed person, my head filled with esoteric military slang and a deep fear of beeping motion detectors. For days afterwards, I slept with my duvet covering my mouth so that no facehuggers could get me. (I was a highly impressionable teenager.)
It’s little wonder that the film has had such a profound effect on video game design. Take the colonial marines, for example. Although the concept of the space soldier had been around in sci-fi novels since the 1930s, most notably in the works of EE “Doc” Smith and Robert Heinlein (the Starship Troopers), Hicks, Hudson, Vasquez and co, were the perfect 80s rendition, combining the witty banter of contemporary buddy cop flicks with awesome weaponry and hi-tech gadgets. Their influence is easy to spot in Doom, where the nameless marine fights ceaseless waves of hellish monsters using a mix of futuristic rifles and good old shotguns. It’s there too in the Halo series, the Spartan soldiers sporting the same armour and mega weapons, cruising about in very similar highly militarised starships and fighting recognisable hive-mind space beasts. Gears of War, Killzone and Marathon all borrow from the same set of costumes and deadly accessories.

articles.author: Zoe Williams
articles.description:
The new breed of camera-equipped streetlights has the potential to fight crime and track down missing persons. Or will it just take Britain one step closer to a surveillance state?
How would you feel if your neighbourhood lamp-posts could recognise your number plate, and also your face? Maybe you wouldn’t mind, given how long we’ve had automatic number plate recognition and CCTV. What about if that lamp-post could power itself through its own solar panels, and perhaps find another use for any extra power generated – that would be good, right? This is what Conflow Power Group (CPG) in Warwickshire claims for its iLamps, the first of their kind in the UK.
What if lamp-posts had the potential to incorporate new AI capability – gait analysis, suspicious behaviours – that you haven’t even heard of? This is what the organisation Big Brother Watch worries about. And what if the home secretary had explicitly said she believed in a “panopticon state” – that is, a state that could watch you at all times (as Shabana Mahmood already has) – and what if she still had a job when the lamp-post eyes got their updates? Or what if the next home secretary was even keener on hyper-surveillance (hard to imagine), and the street apparatus was already in place? What about all the data this would harvest – who would own it?

articles.description:
The debut from Scandinavian outfit Dead Astronauts promises shooting, survival, and, in a shake-up to the genre, seeds that terraform its pristine world right before your eyes
The wilds of the sub-Arctic north: towering pine trees, flashes of psychedelic-yellow lichen, and a sun that never wholly sets during the summer months. This land is gorgeous, yes, but also unforgiving, yet in Haex (pronounced “hex”) you have an unusual tool at your disposal to make it a little more hospitable: a cube that fits snugly in the palm of your hand out of which grows a plant. You plant this so-called Seed in the earth and – voilà – the world around you transforms: new vegetation and topography but also narrative threads to follow, and, naturally, enemies. Wield these small-but-mighty kernels of change at your own peril.
“Your adventure and your world is player-shaped,” says Haex’s creative director Tobias Nyman. He explains that everyone starts a campaign with a unique, procedurally generated world. The horror movie sensation of 2026 has its roots in gaming’s discovery of ‘noclip’ – and the hidden virtual realms that could be opened up inside games. Developers explain how everyone got lost in these liminal spaces
It starts on 4chan, in a May 2019 thread entitled “unsettling images”. The first post was a photo showing an empty room with the now iconic yellow wallpaper, no natural lighting and a kind of inexplicable jutting half-wall. Shortly afterwards, another user (there are no usernames on 4chan, just identifying numbers) responded with 78 words of text that would essentially lay out the blueprint for a future $262m A24 movie sensation.
“If you’re not careful and you noclip out of reality in the wrong areas, you’ll end up in the Backrooms,” the post begins. For the uninitiated, “noclip” refers to a game mode in which collision with solid objects is disabled, allowing players to move freely through walls and floors. Think of Chiwetel Ejiofor’s character in the film, finding a permeable wall in the basement of his furniture store and passing through to the world on the other side.
